quote_orig: However, it is noteworthy that Jesus is here assigned a role in the creation of all things. This is remarkable in one of the earliest Christian texts that we have, because, of all the exclusively divine prerogatives, the act of creation most clearly signaled the absolute distinction between God and all other reality. Jews were in the habit of safeguarding strict monotheism by denying that God had any assistants in the work of creation (cf. Isa. 40:12–13, 44:24). Paul must mean that Jesus Christ was not some created assistant to God but himself belonged eternally to the unique identity of the one God.
context_before: Discussion of Col 1:16 ('all things have been created through [Jesus Christ] and for him') and then of 1 Cor 8:6 ('one Lord, Jesus Christ').
what_it_says: Bauckham argues that Jesus' role in creation places him inside God's unique identity, and calls Colossians 1:16 one of the earliest Christian texts.
claim_supported: (B) earliest Christian texts (timing); (A/B) Jesus belongs to the unique identity of God
scholar_qualification: He argues this from the exegesis of creation texts and the Jewish practice of denying divine assistants; his claim concerns Paul's and the early Christian texts, not a statement by the historical Jesus.

quote_orig: When early Christians worshipped Jesus, they did not see him as an alternative or distinct object of worship alongside God. They included Jesus in their worship of God, much as Paul included Jesus in the Shemaʿ. context_before: Discussion of Phil 2:9-11 and its echo of Isa 45:22-23, where YHWH says 'To me every knee shall bow'.

scholar_qualification: He describes what early Christians thought and did in worship; he does not claim the historical Jesus demanded worship. He also says Paul 'never or hardly ever' calls Jesus 'God' (see the next item).
